_meta.purpose: STOF PII/Sensitive-Data Disclosure Knowledge Base -- real disclosed bug bounty patterns for stof/modules/disclosure_tests.py.
sources: HackerOne #845677 (Imgur) -- sourcemaps and unminified source code exposed
Bugcrowd -- source code leakage due to exposed sourcemap
HackerOne #1624157, #1629822 (U.S. DoD VDP) -- exposed .git folder, dumped via GitTools/gitdumper
HackerOne #2784712 (AWS VDP) -- .env file exposed with directory listing
PortSwigger Web Security Academy -- 'Information disclosure on debug page' lab (HTML comment linking to a debug endpoint that reveals a SECRET_KEY)
HackerOne #1067004 (U.S. Dept of Defense), #397527 (Grab) -- API responses returning sensitive internal fields never rendered by the consuming client
HackerOne #1450014 (Krisp), #1724771 (Yelp) -- robots.txt disclosing internal/admin-shaped paths not otherwise linked from the application
_meta.key_finding: disclosure_tests.py already covers PII surfacing through an app's own normal data flow (API response over-exposure, error-message leakage, IDOR chaining, PII in URLs). The clearest remaining real-world gap is a structurally different class: files and markup that were never meant to be served at all -- build/VCS artifacts left on the webserver (source maps, .git, .env, backup files) and secrets/PII left in HTML comments or inline <script> blocks that render invisibly to a normal user but are plainly visible in raw response source. Both are pure GET-and-inspect, no state-changing writes, no auth-flow assumptions -- a close structural sibling of TC-105.4's existing 'scan a URL string with find_pii()' shape, just scanning file contents/HTML source instead of URLs.

patterns.generalized_transformation: For each discovered JS asset, parse its trailing `//# sourceMappingURL=` comment (or guess `<script-src>.map`) and GET it; separately, GET a small fixed list of well-known sensitive paths at the site root (`/.git/config`, `/.git/HEAD`, `/.env`, `/.env.bak`, `/config.php.bak`) -- no crawl-discovery needed for these, they're checked directly regardless of whether anything links to them.
patterns.abstracted_endpoint_pattern: Any served `*.js` asset (for source maps); the site origin root (for VCS/env/backup files) -- independent of the crawler's discovered endpoint list.
patterns.evidence_signal: Never a bare 200/404 -- a catch-all SPA route can return 200+index.html for any path, so the response BODY must be checked: a `.map` hit requires valid JSON with a non-empty `sources` array containing real-looking file paths (e.g. `webpack://`, `/src/`); a `.git/config` hit requires the literal strings `[core]` and `repositoryformatversion` in the body; a `.env` hit requires at least one `KEY=VALUE`-shaped line whose key matches a secret-ish name pattern (`_KEY`, `_SECRET`, `_PASSWORD`, `_TOKEN`, `DATABASE_URL`).
patterns.real_example: Imgur sourcemaps/unminified JS (HackerOne #845677); DoD VDP exposed .git folders dumped via GitTools (HackerOne #1624157, #1629822); AWS VDP .env exposure with directory listing (HackerOne #2784712).

stof_coverage.notes: Implemented as disclosure_tests.py's _technique_source_map_and_backup_exposure: checks the fixed candidate-path list (/.git/config, /.git/HEAD, /.env, /.env.bak, /config.php.bak) at the discovered origin, plus a .map probe for every discovered .js asset (following its trailing //# sourceMappingURL= comment when present, else a single <script-src>.map fallback attempt), each GET's body checked with a dedicated helper (_looks_like_git_config, _looks_like_env_file, _looks_like_source_map) rather than status code alone. Live-validated against demo.testfire.net (68 discovered endpoints, 1 JS asset checked plus the 5 fixed paths): PASS -- none of the candidate paths or JS source maps were present/accessible on that target.

patterns.generalized_transformation: Fetch a crawled page's RAW HTML response body (not the DOM after JS execution -- must be the literal bytes the server sent, matching what a 'View Source'/curl would show). Extract the contents of every `<!-- ... -->` comment block and every non-`src` inline `<script>` block. Run the same PII regex scan (`find_pii()`) already used for API responses/URLs, plus a small secret-shaped pattern set (AWS-style `AKIA[0-9A-Z]{16}`, generic `api[_-]?key`/`secret` name-value pairs, JWT-shaped `eyJ...` tokens).
patterns.evidence_signal: A PII/secret match found strictly INSIDE a comment or inline-script span -- not merely present anywhere on the page (a value that's already visible in the rendered page text isn't a NEW disclosure via source inspection, it's just TC-105.1/.4's existing pattern in a different location). This distinguishes 'hidden in markup a normal user never sees' from 'visible content that happens to also appear in a script variable.'
patterns.real_example: PortSwigger's 'Information disclosure on debug page' lab -- an HTML comment links to a hidden debug endpoint that reveals a SECRET_KEY environment variable; a well-documented, canonical example of this exact class.

stof_coverage.notes: Implemented as disclosure_tests.py's _technique_pii_in_html_source, backed by the pure find_hidden_disclosures() helper: extracts every <!-- --> comment and non-src inline <script> block from the raw HTML body via regex, then runs find_pii() unchanged plus a new small _SECRET_PATTERNS set (AWS-style AKIA key, JWT-shaped token, generic api_key/secret name-value pair) against those spans only -- PII visible in ordinary rendered page text is deliberately excluded so it isn't double-reported as a new source-inspection finding. Live-validated against demo.testfire.net (55 discovered page endpoints, 15 scanned per the max_endpoints_scanned cap): PASS -- no PII or secret-shaped values found hidden in HTML comments or inline scripts on any scanned page.

patterns.generalized_transformation: For each crawled page endpoint, navigate a real authenticated browser Page to it (a raw HTTP GET/response body cannot see this data at all -- it only ever exists as client-side JS state), then read back `Object.entries(localStorage)` and `Object.entries(sessionStorage)` via `page.evaluate()`. Run the same PII regex scan (`find_pii()`, unchanged) against every stored value string.
patterns.abstracted_endpoint_pattern: Any crawled page endpoint (`endpoint_type == "page"`), navigated post-authentication.
patterns.evidence_signal: A `find_pii()` match found in the VALUE of a `localStorage`/`sessionStorage` key -- the storage key name itself is reported alongside the match label, never the full raw value (same never-log-full-PII discipline as `find_pii()`'s own `PiiMatch.preview` truncation everywhere else in this file).
patterns.real_example: Widely documented real pattern across bug-bounty writeups and OWASP guidance: SPAs caching a logged-in user's profile object (email, name, sometimes a JWT or API token) in `localStorage` 'for convenience' on page reload -- unlike a cookie, `localStorage` has no `httpOnly` equivalent, so it's fully readable by any JS running in that origin, making it a standing, browser-persistent target for any XSS found anywhere else on the same site (OWASP's own 'HTML5 Security Cheat Sheet' calls out exactly this local-storage-is-JS-readable property as the reason not to cache sensitive data there).

stof_coverage.notes: Implemented as disclosure_tests.py's _technique_pii_in_client_storage: the one technique in this file that navigates a real Playwright Page (context.new_page(), same 'needs a real Page not just context.request' precedent as xss_tests.py's TC-128.5 DOM XSS technique) and calls page.evaluate() to read Object.entries(localStorage)/Object.entries(sessionStorage) back into Python, then runs the existing find_pii() unchanged against every stored value. Live-validated against demo.testfire.net as admin (scan_bcb6a0a6, 2026-08-27, 68 discovered endpoints, 55 page endpoints, 15 scanned per max_endpoints_scanned cap): PASS -- no PII found in localStorage/sessionStorage on any scanned page. Same run also reconfirmed TC-105.5 PASS and TC-105.6 PASS, and (unrelated to this technique) flagged TC-105.1 FAIL (PII in /swagger/properties.json) and TC-105.4 FAIL (PII-shaped value in /sendFeedback's URL) -- both pre-existing techniques, not this addition.

patterns.generalized_transformation: Probe a discovered GET API endpoint with the highest-privileged configured role, parse the JSON response, and recursively walk every object key in the parsed structure (not the raw response text) for a sensitive-shaped field NAME -- password/password_hash, ssn, credit_card, api_key, private_key, access_token/refresh_token, is_admin/is_superuser, internal_notes -- regardless of what the field's VALUE looks like. This is deliberately distinct from TC-105.1's PII-value pattern matching: a field named password_hash holding a bcrypt digest matches no PII value pattern at all, but the field itself should never reach a client.
patterns.abstracted_endpoint_pattern: Any discovered endpoint_type=='api', method=='GET' endpoint returning a JSON body.
patterns.evidence_signal: A parsed JSON object contains a key (at any nesting depth) matching the sensitive-field-name list -- checked as an actual object key via json.loads()+recursive walk, never a bare substring match against the raw response text (which would also match the word appearing only inside an unrelated string value).
patterns.real_example: HackerOne #1067004 (DoD) and #397527 (Grab): both describe an API endpoint serializing and returning an entire internal record -- including fields the consuming UI never uses or displays -- rather than an explicitly minimized response shape, the textbook 'excessive data exposure' (API3:2019/API3:2023) pattern.

stof_coverage.note: Implemented in stof/modules/disclosure_tests.py as _technique_excessive_data_exposure, with the pure helper _sensitive_field_names(body) -> set[str] (JSON-parse + recursive key walk, directly unit-tested including a false-positive guard for a sensitive word appearing only in a value, never a key).

patterns.generalized_transformation: Fetch /robots.txt and /sitemap.xml at the target origin (both meant to be public by design, so their mere existence is never a finding) and extract every Disallow: path / <loc> URL. Flag only entries whose path segment itself contains an internal-looking hint word (admin, internal, staging, backup, debug, config, private, console, manage, secret, dev, test) -- a bare 'Disallow: /' or '/images/' is normal and explicitly not flagged.
patterns.evidence_signal: A Disallow/<loc> path contains an internal-looking hint word.
patterns.real_example: HackerOne #1450014 (Krisp) and #1724771 (Yelp): both disclosed reports specifically flag a public robots.txt listing paths that hand an attacker a ready-made map of unlinked/sensitive surface -- exactly the 'this doesn't confirm exploitability, but it removes the need to guess or brute-force' framing this technique uses.

stof_coverage.note: Implemented in stof/modules/disclosure_tests.py as _technique_robots_sitemap_disclosure, with the pure helper _internal_looking_paths(body) -> list[str], directly unit-tested for both the flagged and the not-flagged (benign path) cases.
